text: Rated Medium (revised from Low, since the source does have real data behind it): the ECDE indicator dataset (sis-ecde-climate-indicators on the CDS) provides pre-computed, peer-reviewed indices - e.g. "Hot Days" count, SPI-3 drought index, Fire Weather Index - so, unlike Copernicus CDS, no own index/threshold definition is needed. Still requires geocoding and grid extraction, hence Medium rather than Low.

Advantage over using Copernicus CDS directly: ECDE provides ready-made, peer-reviewed climate hazard indices with documented methodology and academic citations (e.g. Spinoni et al. 2018/2020, Jacob et al. 2013), rather than raw climate variables the bank would need to convert into its own index definitions. Both draw on similar underlying grid resolutions (0.1-0.25 degree, or 5km for hydrology-based indices), so the advantage is in processing effort saved, not in finer raw resolution. Weaker than Copernicus CDS in hazard breadth (permafrost, landslide, soil erosion are not covered at all) and in flexibility (limited to the 32 pre-selected indices).
NUTS-aggregated layers usable directly; finer layers (SHP/raster) require geocoding and spatial overlay.
Well suited to substantive risk determination (col. 0050); over-specified for the pure Geography reporting requirement.

Rated High: the raw fire danger index (GeoTIFF, varies daily) and historical burnt-area layer have no ready-made exposure score, unlike the Low-rated BWV/HQ30 and WLV vector datasets - both require own geocoding, index interpretation and GIS overlay.
Free, CC-BY 4.0 (attribution only).
Raw climate variables (NetCDF grid data) without ready-made risk classification; requires climatological/GIS processing.
Individual sub-datasets may carry stricter terms than the general CC-BY 4.0 - e.g. E-OBS is restricted to non-commercial research/education use only; verify per dataset before use.
Not suitable for populating individual exposures; useful for benchmarking/peer comparison only.
Traceable methodology replicable with AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus; useful methodological anchor, operates at NUTS3 rather than country level.

Single national dataset (HQ30/HQ100/HQ300 flood extent family) with its own INSPIRE Atom download service and WMS/WFS endpoints; requires geocoding of portfolio locations and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate state datasets - the same pipeline shape as the WLV Gefahrenzonenplan.

Covers riverine flood hazard (BWV) with the same subject-matter content as HORA but usable without legal restriction. Scope narrowed to flood: torrent, avalanche and mass-movement hazards are covered nationally and more consistently by the WLV Gefahrenzonenplan.

Rated Low (revised from an earlier Medium rating): a single national shapefile dataset with its own download service; requires geocoding and a standard spatial overlay, but no merging of separate state datasets - consistent with bundeslaender_open_data (BWV/HQ30), which has near-identical technical characteristics.

The strongest national source for mass-movement and torrent hazards: a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz covering torrents, avalanches and erosion processes (rockfall, landslide, debris flow), published as a High Value Dataset. Complements rather than duplicates the BWV flood data, which covers riverine flooding.
High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138; free of charge, bulk download via the WLV download service, ESRI shapefile format.

Design event is an approximately 150-year return period. Zones are process boundaries rather than inundation lines and include erosion processes and sediment transport, so they are not directly comparable to the BWV flood inundation areas.
Suitable for individual address-level checks only, not for systematic portfolio classification.
Good supplementary dataset for chronic risk (water stress), since AT sources primarily cover acute hazards.
Ready-made risk scores per location, directly integrable via API.
High data quality and granularity; cost structure typically not designed for SNCI scale.
Ready-made scores/maps via web tool or API.
Very extensive (scenarios to 2100); commercial, geared towards larger institutions/reinsurers.
Country-level granularity too coarse for exposure/NUTS assignment; useful for plausibility checks only.
Best available current Austrian permafrost source for context/discussion; not suitable for exposure-level classification.

Single CSV file (326,479 records) keyed to the Firmenbuch number; joins directly to a loan portfolio without GIS or geocoding work. Codes are 5-digit OeNACE; the 4-digit NACE level required by D 01.01 is obtained by dropping the last digit.

The strongest transition-risk source identified: official assignment under section 21 Bundesstatistikgesetz, published as a High Value Dataset under CC BY 4.0, covering all actively registered Austrian companies with an assigned economic activity. Resolves the previous trade-off in which official quality and open access were mutually exclusive.
CC BY 4.0, published under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 (High Value Datasets); free of charge, bulk download, updated continuously.

Verified as OeNACE 2025 / NACE Rev. 2.1 by structural analysis of the 682 distinct codes: division 45 absent (abolished in Rev. 2.1), classes 47.41/47.42/47.43 absent (merged into 47.40), class 46.89 present (newly created in Rev. 2.1), and divisions 62 and 63 following the Rev. 2.1 structure. Template D 01.01 uses the same revision, as evidenced by its designation K.63 for computing infrastructure, which is only valid under Rev. 2.1. No transcoding between classification versions is therefore required.
Ready-made OeNACE 2025 classification per entity, delivered via API; no manual extract handling required.

Retained alongside the HVD dataset because access already exists institutionally in parts of the Austrian banking sector (for example across the Raiffeisen sector), making the marginal cost zero and an existing query operationally simpler than downloading and joining the HVD file. Adds daily currency and coverage beyond the Firmenbuch.

technical_effort reflects the effort to access and use the source's own data (dashboard-only, no download/API, same interface as EBA ESG Dashboard, hence Low). The separate, substantially higher effort of replicating the ECB's methodology with AnaCredit/JRC/Copernicus-equivalent inputs is a distinct undertaking and is described in the abstract, not folded into this column.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query or download the relevant pre-computed ECDE indicator (sis-ecde-climate-indicators dataset on the CDS) for the coordinate. (3) Assign the returned value to the exposure. Automatable, but resolution varies by indicator (5km to ~28km), so multiple exposures within the same grid cell share a value.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Identify the NUTS2/3 region for each coordinate. (3) Download/query the relevant hazard module(s) via API or shapefile. (4) Join exposures to their region's value. Regional (not parcel-level) result.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WMS/WFS or download the GeoTIFF fire danger index / burnt-area layer. (3) Extract the raster cell value at each coordinate (point-in-raster lookup). (4) Decide how to handle the time-varying daily index (e.g. seasonal maximum or long-run average) to arrive at a single static attribute per exposure.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Select and download the relevant climate variable(s) in NetCDF/GRIB. (3) Derive a hazard-relevant indicator from the raw climate variable (this is a climatological modelling step, not a simple lookup). (4) Extract the grid-cell value at each coordinate.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WFS endpoint (nz-core:HazardArea) with each coordinate, or download the GML/shapefile once and perform a local spatial join. (3) Assign the returned zone/extent value to the exposure. Fully automatable, parcel-level result.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the WMS/WFS endpoint or download the shapefile/GeoPackage once and perform a local spatial join. (3) Assign the returned zone value to the exposure. Fully automatable, parcel-level result within mapped municipalities.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Download the watershed-level dataset (CSV/GeoPackage) or query the API. (3) Perform a spatial join to the relevant watershed polygon. (4) Assign the watershed's indicator value to the exposure. Automatable, but resolution is watershed- not parcel-level.
Send exposure coordinates/address to the API; receive a facility-level score directly. No further spatial processing required.
Send exposure coordinates/address to the API; receive a facility-level score directly. No further spatial processing required.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Determine the ADM2 (district) administrative unit for each coordinate. (3) Query the ThinkHazard! API for the hazard level of that district (or download the relevant Risk Data Library dataset for gridded hazards such as landslide and perform a spatial join). (4) Assign the returned district-level value to the exposure. Automatable, but resolution is district- not parcel-level.
Bulk-download the CSV and join directly on Firmenbuchnummer against the loan portfolio. No geocoding or spatial processing needed.
Send the Firmenbuchnummer or company identifier to the API; receive the OeNACE classification directly. No further processing required.

Climate-ADAPT is a public knowledge portal operated by the European Environment Agency (EEA) (EEA, n.d.-a). It hosts the European Climate Data Explorer (ECDE), which provides 32 pre-computed, peer-reviewed climate hazard indices covering 16 hazard categories, grouped into six IPCC AR6 climatic-impact-driver types (heat and cold, wet and dry, wind, snow and ice, coastal, open ocean); the indicator dataset itself is published on the Copernicus Climate Data Store as a distinct, downloadable/queryable dataset (EEA/C3S, n.d.). Not all of the matrix's physical hazards are represented: permafrost, landslide and soil erosion have no corresponding index in this set, while heat stress and water stress are only indirectly covered via proxy indices (Universal Thermal Climate Index; aridity) (EEA, 2021). Grid resolution varies by indicator, from 5km (hydrology-based indices such as river flood and aridity) to roughly 0.1-0.25 degrees (~11-28km) for most temperature, precipitation, wind and fire-weather indices (EEA/C3S, n.d.). The source is accessed through an interactive web portal, a queryable API and direct download of the underlying indicator dataset, and is free to use. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source.

The Risk Data Hub (RDH) is a public multi-hazard risk and loss data platform operated by the Joint Research Centre (JRC) in cooperation with the EU Disaster Risk Management Knowledge Centre (DRMKC) (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). It provides modelled exposure, hazard and historical-event data covering multiple physical hazards at regional (NUTS 2/3) granularity across EU, EFTA and IPA countries (JRC DRMKC, n.d.). The source is accessed through a web map portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source and secondary to the Geography dimension (0090–0130).

EFFIS is a public wildfire information service operated jointly by the JRC and Copernicus Emergency Management Service (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). It provides daily fire danger indices and historical burnt-area data covering wildfire risk at grid/raster granularity across Europe and the MENA region (JRC/Copernicus EMS, n.d.). The source is accessed through an OGC map service and direct download, and is free of charge under a CC-BY 4.0 licence requiring attribution only. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source.

The CDS is a public climate data repository operated by ECMWF on behalf of the EU (ECMWF, n.d.), comprising over 140 datasets of raw and derived climate variables and reanalysis/projection data. This entry covers the general-purpose raw variables (e.g. ERA5 temperature, precipitation, wind fields); the standalone, ready-made hazard indicator products hosted on the same CDS (ERA5-HEAT for heat stress, the SMHI hydrology dataset for flood/water stress/soil-moisture drought, CEMS Fire Danger for wildfire) are documented separately under copernicus_climate_indicators, since they differ materially in processing effort and portfolio-readiness. The source is accessed through a web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge, uniformly licensed under CC-BY 4.0 since July 2025 (individual sub-datasets may carry stricter terms). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source and secondary to the Geography dimension.

The EBA ESG Dashboard is a public statistics dashboard operated by the European Banking Authority (EBA) (EBA, n.d.-a). It provides aggregated ESG risk indicators at EU bank level, covering both physical and transition risk dimensions at institution/portfolio-level granularity rather than individual exposure level (EBA, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a web-based statistics dashboard and is free to use. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant only as a benchmarking reference, not to any specific data point.

This is a public methodological and statistical resource operated by the European Central Bank (ECB) (ECB, n.d.). It provides a documented methodology and euro-area statistics on physical risk exposure, covering physical hazards at institution/portfolio-level granularity (NUTS3-based underlying methodology) (ECB, n.d.). The source is accessed through a statistics dashboard and is free to use, though the underlying data (AnaCredit/RIAD) are not accessible to an SNCI. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a secondary source.

This is a national flood extent dataset, published via the INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, with the Bundesministerium fuer Land- und Forstwirtschaft, Klima- und Umweltschutz, Regionen und Wasserwirtschaft (BMLUK) as data owner and Umweltbundesamt GmbH as the technical operator (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). It combines Abflussuntersuchungen (ABU), HORA data and, in part, the BWV and WLV hazard zoning plans into a single set of flood extent layers for the 30-, 100- and 300-year return periods, covering flood risk at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through OGC WMS/WFS services and direct GML/shapefile download via the INSPIRE Atom download service, and is free of charge under a CC BY 4.0 licence. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

The GZP is a public national hazard zoning dataset operated by the Forsttechnischer Dienst fuer Wildbach- und Lawinenverbauung (Federal Ministry BMLUK) (data.gv.at, n.d.-b). It provides a statutory hazard assessment under the Forstgesetz covering torrent, avalanche, landslide and erosion processes at parcel/address-level granularity across Austria (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through an OGC map service and direct download in shapefile/GeoPackage format, and is free of charge as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138 (INSPIRE Geoportal Oesterreich, n.d.-a). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

HORA (Natural Hazard Overview and Risk Assessment Austria) is a publicly accessible Austrian WebGIS application, operated by the Land-, Forst- und Wasserwirtschaftliche Rechenzentrum (LFRZ) on behalf of the responsible federal ministry (LFRZ, n.d.). It provides address- and cadastral-level initial information on natural hazards, currently covering flood, earthquake, storm, hail and snow (HORA, n.d.), with further hazards such as landslide added over time through cooperation with GeoSphere Austria (BMLUK, n.d.). The source is accessed through an interactive web interface via individual location queries, and is free to use. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

The Aqueduct Water Risk Atlas is a public water-risk dataset operated by the World Resources Institute (WRI) (WRI, n.d.). It provides 13 modelled indicators covering water stress, drought risk and both riverine and coastal flood risk at sub-catchment (watershed) granularity globally (WRI, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a web map portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source.

This is a commercial dataset operated by Moody's ESG Solutions (Moody's, n.d.). The underlying methodology originates from Four Twenty Seven, Inc., a physical-climate-risk data firm founded in 2012, in which Moody's Corporation acquired a majority stake in July 2019 as a Moody's Investors Service affiliate (Moody's, 2019); the acquisition was reported in Moody's own 2019 Form 10-Q as operating within the MIS reportable segment (Moody's, 2019b). It provides proprietary modelled physical climate risk scores covering six hazards (floods, heat stress, hurricanes and typhoons, sea-level rise, water stress, wildfires) at facility/object-level granularity globally (Moody's, n.d.-b); note that the storm hazard is modelled as tropical cyclones specifically, which has limited relevance to Austria. The source is accessed through a commercial analytics platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a commercial licence agreement. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source.

NATHAN Risk Suite is a commercial dataset operated by Munich Re (Munich Re, n.d.). It provides proprietary modelled natural hazard and climate scenario scores covering multiple hazards at facility/object-level granularity globally, including scenarios extending to 2100 (Munich Re, n.d.). Two access models exist: a subscription-based portfolio platform (Business/Corporate tiers, with API access, quote-based pricing) and a subscription-free, pay-per-location "On-Demand" service priced from EUR 100-160 per location depending on package size (Munich Re, n.d.-c). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source.

This is a public dataset collection operated by the World Bank Group in cooperation with GFDRR (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.), comprising both the historical-event Risk Data Library and the forward-looking, probabilistic ThinkHazard! hazard tool (GFDRR, n.d.). It provides climate and disaster risk data covering multiple hazards, with ThinkHazard! resolving to district (ADM2) level via a public API and the Risk Data Library varying by dataset (GFDRR, n.d.-b), and a development-country focus overall (World Bank/GFDRR, n.d.). The source is accessed through a generic web portal, direct download and an API, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant only as a context/validation reference, not to a specific data point.

KryoMon.AT is a publicly funded research consortium coordinated by the University of Graz, involving multiple Austrian universities, the Austrian and Bavarian Academies of Sciences, GeoSphere Austria and several associations (KryoMon.AT, n.d.; ORF Steiermark, 2026). It provides periodic reports on permafrost, glacier and snow trends covering permafrost hazard at station-based granularity across selected Austrian alpine sites (KryoMon.AT, n.d.). The source is accessed through a reports/publications website and PDF downloads, and is free of charge. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a secondary source.

This is a public register operated by Statistik Austria (Statistik Austria, n.d.). It provides the official OeNACE 2025 (NACE Rev. 2.1) economic-activity code for each Austrian company, keyed to the Firmenbuch number, covering the full national company register at entity-level granularity (Statistik Austria, n.d.). The source is accessed through direct bulk download in CSV format and is free of charge under a CC BY 4.0 licence, published as a High Value Dataset under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2023/138. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to the NACE subsector dimension as a primary source.

Wirtschafts-Compass is a commercial Austrian company-data service operated by Compass-Verlag GmbH (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). It provides an editorially enriched OeNACE classification per entity, covering the Austrian company landscape at entity-level granularity, delivered with daily currency (Compass-Verlag, n.d.). The source is accessed through an API and a web portal, and is paid, though the operator states that the finance and insurance sector is among its long-standing customers, meaning many Austrian banking-sector institutions may already hold an institutional licence (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-b). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to the NACE subsector dimension as a secondary source.

Coverage was originally set uniformly to "partial" across 10 of 12 matrix hazards with identical granularity text, without per-hazard verification. Verified against the EEA's own 32-index / 16-hazard / 6-category index set (EEA, 2021): permafrost, landslide and soil erosion are not represented at all and were corrected to "none"; heat_stress and water_stress are only indirect proxies (UTCI; aridity), not dedicated categories; and the true resolution of the source's own report table is three European macro-regions, not NUTS 1/2 as previously stated.

Originally soil_erosion=full, glacial_lake=partial, heat_stress=partial, water_stress=partial with uniform reasoning. Verified against the JRC's own 2023 technical report (JRC136527, Table 5 "List of hazards addressed currently on the RDH"): only River flood, Coastal flood, Earthquake, Landslide, Forest fire and Subsidence have a modelled Risk Analysis layer. "Subsidence" is a physically distinct process from soil erosion, so soil_erosion corrected to none. glacial_lake, heat_stress and water_stress do not appear in either the Risk Analysis or Loss Data catalogues and were corrected to none. storm, heavy_precip, heat_wave and drought remain partial but are now documented as historical loss-record coverage only (Loss Data module), not modelled hazard layers.

Originally heat_stress=full and wildfire=partial. Verified: CDS hosts the same shared EEA/C3S 32-index dataset as Climate-ADAPT (sis-ecde-climate-indicators), so heat_stress is only the same UTCI proxy noted for Climate-ADAPT and was corrected to partial for consistency. wildfire was corrected to full after confirming a dedicated, purpose-built "Fire danger indices historical data" dataset (CEMS/EFFIS, ERA5-driven, three national fire-danger rating systems) is directly downloadable from the CDS, not merely derivable from raw variables.

Originally landslide=none, heavy_precip=none, drought=partial, wildfire=partial, heat_stress=full. Verified against the ECB's own indicator methodology page, which explicitly lists: "coastal flooding, river flooding, wildfires, landslides, subsidence, windstorms, water stress, droughts and rainfall variation." landslide was missing entirely and corrected to full; drought and wildfire were under-rated and corrected to full; heavy_precip (rainfall variation) corrected from none to partial. heat_stress corrected from full to partial: not named among the ECB's own 9 listed hazards, despite other ECB communications describing "heat and water stress" as a chronic risk category - flagged as a documentation inconsistency pending clarification.

Originally flood, landslide, storm, heat_wave, drought, water_stress and wildfire were all uniformly partial, and soil_erosion was partial. Verified against GFDRR's ThinkHazard! methodology documentation and the World Bank/GFDRR Global Landslide Hazard Map: flood, heat_wave (extreme heat), water_stress (water scarcity, via a dedicated Water Stress Index) and wildfire have commonly-available probabilistic hazard data and were corrected to full; landslide is covered via a dedicated gridded global dataset and corrected to full. soil_erosion, heat_stress and heavy_precip do not appear as distinct categories anywhere in the ThinkHazard!/Risk Data Library ecosystem and were corrected to none. storm remains partial because ThinkHazard!'s "cyclone" hazard model is tropical-cyclone-oriented and its applicability to European extratropical windstorms was not confirmed. drought remains partial as it is only indirectly inferable from the water-scarcity index, not a distinct event-based drought product.

Originally flood and drought were rated partial. Verified against WRI's own 13-indicator Aqueduct 4.0 framework: dedicated "riverine flood risk" (rfr), "coastal flood risk" (cfr) and "drought risk" (drr) indicators exist by name, not merely inferred from water-stress data, and were corrected to full.

Originally storm=full, heat_wave=full, drought=full, wildfire=partial. Verified against Moody's own consistently published hazard list (floods, heat stress, hurricanes and typhoons, sea-level rise, water stress, wildfires): storm was corrected to none because Moody's names "hurricanes and typhoons" specifically - a tropical-cyclone hazard not applicable to landlocked Austria; heat_wave corrected to none because only "heat stress" (a distinct, chronic indicator) is named, not a separate acute heat-wave product; drought corrected to none as it does not appear in any published Moody's hazard list found; wildfire corrected to full as it is consistently and explicitly named.

Originally soil_erosion=partial, glacial_lake=partial, landslide=partial, heavy_precip/heat_wave/heat_stress/drought/water_stress=full, wildfire=partial. Verified against Munich Re's own 15-hazard "Natural Hazards Edition" list (River Flood, Flash Flood, Storm Surge, Tropical Cyclone, Extratropical Storm, Hail, Tornado, Lightning, Earthquake, Volcano, Tsunami, Wildfire, Avalanche, Landslide, Subsidence): landslide and wildfire corrected to full (explicitly named); soil_erosion and glacial_lake corrected to none (not covered, or - for soil_erosion - only the physically distinct "Subsidence" is covered). heavy_precip, heat_wave, heat_stress, drought and water_stress were downgraded from full to partial: these are not named in the Natural Hazards Edition, and the separate "Climate Change Edition" advertises "13 climate hazards" without naming them individually in the materials reviewed, so full coverage could not be confirmed.

Specific pricing for Moody's physical risk/Climate on Demand data is not publicly disclosed; access is quote-based via direct sales contact. Public aggregate spend estimates exist for Moody's software generally (third-party benchmarking, not company-published), but these cover unrelated products (e.g. EDF-X, Orbis) and are not specific to the physical risk data product, so they are not usable as a cost estimate here.

Two distinct access models exist. (1) Location Risk Intelligence On-Demand: a subscription-free, pay-per-location service for single-location lookups (not full portfolios), priced in tiered packages from EUR 160 per location (5-location package, EUR 800 net) down to EUR 100 per location (50-location package, EUR 5,000 net; 48 credits per location lookup), prices exclude VAT (Munich Re, n.d.-c). (2) The portfolio-scale Natural Hazards Edition / Climate Change Edition subscription (Business/Corporate tiers, with API access) remains quote-based and not publicly priced.

Pay-per-query pricing: from EUR 6 (excl. VAT) per quarter for up to 10 queries via the WKO-member Wirtschafts-Compass service (Compass-Verlag's own price list) (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-c); individual/basic access starts from EUR 24 per year per the operator's own website (Compass-Verlag, n.d.-d). Official Firmenbuch extract fees (per the Justizministerium's Gebührenverordnung) are billed separately and are not part of the Wirtschafts-Compass subscription cost itself.

Most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets are published under Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication (CC0 1.0), free for any use including commercial, per the operator's own repository documentation (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.); the exact licence tag should be confirmed per-dataset on the dataset landing page before productive use.

Most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets are published under Creative Commons Public Domain Dedication (CC0 1.0), free for any use including commercial, per the operator's own repository documentation (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.); the exact licence tag should be confirmed per-dataset on the dataset landing page before productive use.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the GeoSphere Austria grid API with the coordinates for the relevant SPARTACUS variable(s) (temperature, precipitation). (3) Apply a chosen threshold/index definition (e.g. a heat-wave or heavy-precipitation definition) to the returned time series. (4) Assign the resulting value to the exposure. Fully automatable, 1km grid resolution.

(1) Geocode exposure addresses to coordinates. (2) Query the GeoSphere Austria grid API with the coordinates for the WINFORE SPEI variable at the desired aggregation window (30/90/365 days). (3) Assign the returned SPEI value to the exposure. Fully automatable, 1km grid resolution.

SPARTACUS-v3 is a public gridded climate dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria, the Austrian federal institute for geology, geophysics, climatology and meteorology (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). It provides observed daily, monthly and quarterly temperature, precipitation and sunshine-duration fields at 1km resolution across Austria since 1961, updated daily (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-a). The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge, published under the CC0 1.0 Public Domain Dedication used for most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

WINFORE is a public gridded drought-index dataset operated by GeoSphere Austria (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). It provides the Standardized Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI) at 30-, 90- and 365-day aggregation windows, plus potential evapotranspiration, derived from SPARTACUS temperature and precipitation fields at 1km resolution across Austria, updated daily (GeoSphere Austria, n.d.-b). The source is accessed through a web interface, a coordinate-based REST API and HTTP bulk download, and is free of charge, published under the CC0 1.0 Public Domain Dedication used for most GeoSphere Austria Data Hub datasets (GeoSphere Austria/re3data, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

Not publicly disclosed by Climate X directly. Third-party industry comparison sources estimate EUR 20,000-60,000 per year for portfolios of 30-100 assets, described as "mid-market" pricing relative to enterprise platforms like Jupiter Intelligence or Moody's; this figure is a third-party estimate, not confirmed by the operator (Repath, n.d.).
Send exposure coordinates/address to the Spectra API; receive an asset-level hazard/financial-loss score directly. No further spatial processing required.

Jupiter's own CEO, Rich Sorkin, stated in a 2022 interview that "subscription pricing ranges from $25,000 to multimillion-dollar contracts" depending on scope (Trellis/Clancy, 2022) - the most directly-attributable figure found for this source, though still not a public price list. Third-party industry comparison sources separately describe full portfolio deployments as typically six-figure annual commitments, consistent with the CEO's stated range (Repath, n.d.; SmartResilience, n.d.).
Send exposure coordinates/address to the ClimateScore Global API; receive an asset-level hazard/financial-loss score directly. No further spatial processing required.

Spectra is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Climate X Ltd, a UK-based company founded in 2020 (Technology Tools, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and financial loss projections across up to 16 hazards (including flooding, storms, tropical cyclones, storm surge, heat stress, wildfires, landslides and subsidence), with scenario projections to 2100 (Repath, n.d.; Net Zero Compare, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a quote-based commercial licence; third-party estimates (not operator-confirmed) suggest a "mid-market" price range of roughly EUR 20,000-60,000 per year for a 30-100 asset portfolio (Repath, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source.

ClimateScore Global is a commercial physical climate risk platform operated by Jupiter Intelligence, Inc., a US company founded in 2017 (aigreentools.com, n.d.). It provides asset-level modelled physical hazard scores and finance-grade loss metrics across 9 physical perils (including flood, heat, drought, tropical cyclones, wind and wildfire), across 3 emissions scenarios in 5-year increments to 2100, based on peer-reviewed CMIP6/ERA5 science (aigreentools.com, n.d.). The source is accessed through a commercial SaaS platform and an API, and is paid, subject to a quote-based enterprise licence; Jupiter's own CEO has stated subscription pricing ranges from USD 25,000 to multi-million-dollar contracts depending on scope, with full portfolio deployments typically at six-figure annual commitments (Trellis/Clancy, 2022; Repath, n.d.). In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data points 0050 and 0090–0130 as a primary source.

Split out from copernicus_cds (Aug 2026 revision) because these specific products - unlike the bulk of Copernicus CDS, which requires own processing of raw climate variables - are standalone, ready-made, documented hazard indicators with their own CDS catalogue pages and named producing institutions. Treating them as part of the generic "copernicus_cds" entry would have understated their portfolio-readiness and overstated their technical effort.

This is a set of standalone, ready-made physical hazard indicator products, published as individual datasets on the Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS), distinct from the general-purpose raw climate variables covered by the separate copernicus_cds entry (ECMWF, n.d.). It comprises: ERA5-HEAT (UTCI/heat stress, peer-reviewed, ECMWF), the SMHI hydrology dataset (flood, water stress/aridity, soil-moisture drought, produced by the Swedish Meteorological and Hydrological Institute for C3S), and CEMS Fire Danger (wildfire, produced by JRC/Copernicus Emergency Management Service) (Di Napoli et al., 2021; SMHI/C3S, n.d.). Each is directly downloadable and queryable via the CDS API, and is free to use under CC-BY 4.0-equivalent terms. In the context of Template D 01.01, it is relevant to data point 0050 as a primary source.

Only covers 5 of 12 matrix hazards (heat_stress, flood, water_stress, drought via soil moisture, wildfire); meteorological (SPI-3) drought and the temperature/precipitation/wind-based ECDE indices (heat_wave, heavy_precip, storm) are not available as standalone products - only via copernicus_cds raw variables or the Climate-ADAPT-curated bundle.

EFFIS has been a component of the Copernicus Emergency Management Service since 2015 (effis.jrc.ec.europa.eu now redirects to forest-fire.emergency.copernicus.eu). It is organisationally related to, but distinct from, the "CEMS Fire Danger historical" dataset credited under copernicus_climate_indicators: that dataset is only the ERA5-driven meteorological fire-danger reconstruction, hosted on the CDS for bulk API access, whereas EFFIS additionally provides the observed European Fire Database (~2 million individual fire records) and its own portal-based applications (Current Situation Viewer, Wildfire Risk Viewer, etc.), not available via the CDS.
